title: Though the Fig Tree Does Not Bud
summary: Habakkuk prays that God will renew his mighty deeds and, in wrath, remember mercy. He then describes God coming from the south in blazing glory, shaking mountains and nations, riding against rivers and sea, and going out to save his people and his anointed. Trembling at what he has heard, the prophet resolves to wait quietly for the day of distress to fall on the invaders, and declares that even if every crop and flock fails, he will rejoice in the God of his salvation.
story: Chapters 1 and 2 were an argument. Habakkuk complained about injustice, was told that Babylon was coming, protested that Babylon was worse, and was told to wait for the vision and to live by faith, while Babylon's own crimes would bring it down. Chapter 3 is the prophet's response. He does not receive a timetable or a full explanation. Instead he remembers who God is and what he has done, above all at the exodus and Sinai, and that memory reshapes how he faces the future. The book that began with how long ends with yet I will exult, and the movement from protest to trust is the book's real resolution.
historical:
The chapter looks forward to the Babylonian invasion that Habakkuk has been told is coming, which fell on Judah in stages: the first deportation in 597 BC and the destruction of Jerusalem and its temple in 587 or 586 BC. Verse 16 shows a prophet who knows the day of distress is near and who resolves to wait for God's judgment on the invaders, which came in 539 BC when Persia took Babylon. Verse 17 describes what an invasion meant for an agricultural people: fig trees, vines, olive groves, fields, sheep, and cattle were the whole economy, and armies stripped them bare.

The poem's picture of God's coming draws on Israel's oldest memories. Teman was a region of Edom, and Mount Paran lay in the wilderness south of Judah; both belong to the territory through which Israel traveled after the exodus. Other ancient poems also describe the LORD marching from the south, from Sinai, Seir, and Paran (Deuteronomy 33:2, Judges 5:4-5, Psalm 68:7-8). Cushan appears as a people's name only here, paired with Midian, and probably names a people of the same southern desert region. Many scholars think the poem may preserve very old poetic language, reused by Habakkuk in his prayer.
cultural:
The heading and closing notes show that this prayer was meant to be sung. Shigionoth is an uncertain musical or literary term, related to the heading of Psalm 7; it may indicate a certain kind of lament or a style of performance. Selah, which appears three times, is a term found mostly in the Psalms whose meaning is also uncertain, perhaps a pause or an instrumental interlude. The note to the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, matches the headings of many psalms and suggests the prayer was used in Israel's worship.

The images of God as a warrior riding horses and chariots against rivers and sea drew on language that neighboring peoples used for their storm gods, who fought the sea and the forces of chaos. Israel's poets borrowed the imagery to proclaim that the LORD, not any other god, commands creation. For Israel, the image also recalled the parting of the sea at the exodus and the crossing of the Jordan. The sun and moon standing still in verse 11 echo Joshua 10:12-13. Plague and pestilence walking before and after God (verse 5) picture them as his attendants, a way of saying that even these terrors serve him. Deer were admired for their sure footing on rocky heights, and the closing image appears also in Psalm 18:33.
literary: The chapter is a psalm in three movements. Verse 2 is a petition: Habakkuk has heard of God's deeds and asks him to renew them, and to remember mercy in wrath. Verses 3 to 15 are a theophany, a poetic description of God appearing, told first in the third person (verses 3 to 7) and then in direct address to God (verses 8 to 15). The poem moves from God's coming in radiant light, to the trembling of creation and nations, to battle against rivers and sea, and finally to the purpose of it all: You went forth for the salvation of Your people. Verses 16 to 19 return to the prophet, who trembles at what he has heard and then makes his confession of trust. Verse 17 builds a list of six failures (fig, vine, olive, field, sheep, and cattle) before the turn of verse 18: yet I will exult.

outline.t: Title: a prayer according to Shigionoth
God comes from Teman in radiant glory
The divine warrior goes out to save his people
Though everything fails, I will rejoice in God

doctrines.note: Verses 17 to 19 show what living by faith (2:4) looks like: joy in God that does not depend on harvests, flocks, or visible success. Faith rests on God's character and past faithfulness when present evidence is absent.
The whole theophany is aimed at salvation: God goes forth to save his people and his anointed. God's power over creation and nations serves his purpose of rescue.
Habakkuk prays using memory. He recalls God's past deeds and asks God to act that way again. His prayer holds together honest fear (verse 16) and confident trust (verse 18).
The prophet does not deny the coming loss; he names it in detail. His joy is not a denial of suffering but a choice to find his strength in God within it.

words.note: Racham, to have compassion or show mercy, related to the word for womb. In verse 2 the BSB renders the plea In Your wrath, remember mercy. Habakkuk does not ask God to cancel judgment, which he knows is coming; he asks that God's compassion be present within it.

Yesha, salvation or deliverance, used three times in the chapter. God goes forth for the salvation of his people and to save his anointed (verse 13), and he is the God of my salvation (verse 18); the closely related word yeshuah names his chariots of salvation in verse 8. The word ties God's mighty acts in history to the prophet's personal trust.

Mashiach, anointed one. In verse 13 God goes forth to save Your anointed. In its setting the word most likely refers to Israel's king, anointed with oil at his installation, or to the people as a whole. It is the word from which the title Messiah comes, though here it is not a prediction of a future figure.

Gil, to rejoice or be glad, often with the sense of exuberant celebration. It stands next to the verb exult in verse 18. Coming right after the list of failed crops and empty stalls, it is a joy chosen and grounded in God, not produced by circumstances.

christ: The prayer's portrait of God going forth to save his people and his anointed belongs to the long biblical story of the divine warrior who rescues his people, a story the New Testament sees completed in Jesus. The anointed of verse 13 was Israel's king or people, not a prediction of the Messiah, but the Gospels present Jesus as the Anointed One through whom God's saving purpose for Israel's king is fulfilled. Verse 13 also describes God crushing the head of the house of the wicked, language some readers connect thematically with the promise of Genesis 3:15 that the serpent's head would be crushed, which the New Testament applies to Christ's victory (Romans 16:20). The closing confession has deep resonance with the New Testament's picture of Christian joy: Paul could say he had learned to be content in plenty and in want (Philippians 4:11-13), and he describes believers as sorrowful yet always rejoicing (2 Corinthians 6:10). The link is not prediction but pattern: joy rooted in God rather than in circumstances, which the New Testament grounds in the risen Christ.

hard.q: Is the picture of God as a warrior who threshes nations in anger compatible with the God of love?
hard.a: The imagery of verses 8 to 15 is drawn from ancient warfare and storm poetry, and some readers find it troubling. Several considerations help. The poem's purpose is stated in verse 13: God goes forth to save his people from oppressors. In the Bible's framework, God's anger is directed at evil that destroys, and the divine warrior fights on behalf of the helpless. The imagery is also heavily poetic, drawing on the memory of the exodus, and many of its details describe God's power over creation (rivers, sea, mountains) rather than human slaughter. Some interpreters emphasize that the New Testament reinterprets the warrior image, presenting Christ as conquering through the cross rather than the sword while still looking toward a final judgment. Others stress continuity: the God who judges evil and the God who loves are the same, and a love indifferent to oppression would not be love. Readers differ on how to weigh the violent imagery, but the chapter itself frames it as the power of rescue.

questions: Habakkuk asks God to remember mercy in wrath, knowing judgment is coming. How might you pray when you know hard times are ahead?
The prophet recalls what God did in the past to find strength for the future. What memories of God's faithfulness, in Scripture or in your own life, do you return to?
Verses 17 and 18 describe joy in God when everything else fails. Is that kind of joy possible for you, and what would have to be true of God for it to make sense?
